name: Millenáris Park
description: A park of nearly six hectares in Buda's 2nd district, built around the former Ganz electrical works. Preserved factory halls now serve as event spaces and the National Dance Theatre, while the newer Széllkapu Park adds walkways, solar-topped pavilions and a suspended garden that, according to the official site, looks towards Margit körút and the Castle District.

children.text: Millenáris sits on the site of the Ganz electrical works in Buda's 2nd district. Ábrahám Ganz founded the Ganz foundry in Buda in 1844, and after his death András Mechwart developed the firm and set up its electricity department in 1878. The Lövőház Street building, completed in 1897, employed over 2,000 people, and a large assembly line was built in 1911 and 1912. The firm declined in the later 20th century, and from 2000 it operated as Ganz Transelektro.

The park was created from the former central factory. Demolition of two high-rise buildings began on 12 August 2000, and the park opened in 2001. Two of the old halls, the Great Hall (Building B) and Building D, were kept; together with a new entrance building and an underground car park they form one of the country's largest exhibition halls. Machinery from the old works is still on display. In 2002 the design received the Europa Nostra Award for the way it revived the historic factory halls.

Millenáris has hosted well-known exhibitions, among them Dreamers of Dreams in 2001 and 2002, House of the Future from 2005 to 2007 and the Palace of Wonders series, which ran on the site from 2005 to 2012. The former factory assembly hall, Building E, is now the National Dance Theatre, designed by ZDA - Zoboki Építésziroda, with two theatre halls, a chamber hall and rehearsal rooms.

Széllkapu Park is the newer part. Its walkways lead to three mushroom-shaped buildings topped with solar panels that generate energy and provide shade, and a suspended garden, reached by a panoramic lift, offers views towards Margit körút, the Castle District and the Buda Hills, according to the official Millenáris site. The official site describes the area as barrier-free; pets are not allowed except certified assistance animals. The address is Kis Rókus utca 16-20.
Good to know
Millenáris is on Kis Rókus utca, close to Margit körút, so it combines easily with the Buda side of the Danube.
Check the official Millenáris site for current opening times, events and tickets, because hours differ between the park areas and the venues.
Pets are not allowed except certified assistance animals, according to the official site.

historyIntro: Millenáris occupies the site of the Ganz electrical works in Buda, one of Hungary's best-known industrial firms. After the factory declined, its central works were converted into a park and cultural centre that opened in 2001.

children.text: Ábrahám Ganz founded an iron foundry in Buda in 1844, on the site where the Foundry Museum stands today. After his death András Mechwart developed the firm and set up its electricity department in 1878. The works moved first to Kacsa Street and then to the former Király-malom main street building, and the Lövőház Street building, completed in 1897, employed over 2,000 people. In 1906 the electrical business became independent as Ganz Electricity Co., and a large assembly line was built in 1911 and 1912.

The company suffered from international competition after 1929 but led domestic electrification from the 1920s, until the Second World War cut its renewed success short. After the war it became independent again in 1949 as Ganz Electricity Factory, renamed Ganz Electricity Works in 1963. The firm then declined, and a 1991 joint venture with foreign capital, Ganz Ansaldo, did not stop production from falling. The Budapest factory was relocated to the countryside, and from 2000 the firm operated as Ganz Transelektro.

The Millenáris Foundation was established in 1996, and the former industrial site at Lövőház Street was turned into a cultural and educational centre linked to the thousandth anniversary of the Hungarian state. Demolition of two high-rise buildings began on 12 August 2000 and removed about 120,000 cubic metres of debris, including 2,500 to 3,000 tonnes of steel structures. Building B, the Great Hall, and Building D were kept, and the assembly hall, Building E, was preserved. The park opened in 2001, and in 2002 the design won the Europa Nostra Award for reviving the historic factory halls.

The site soon became known for large exhibitions: Dreamers of Dreams in 2001 and 2002, House of the Future from 2005 to 2007, and the Palace of Wonders series, which ran there from 2005 to 2012. Building E, the former assembly hall, is now the National Dance Theatre, designed by ZDA - Zoboki Építésziroda. The newer Széllkapu Park, with its solar-topped pavilions and suspended garden, later received awards from the Hungarian Urban Planning Association and in the landscape architecture category of the Hungarian Real Estate Development Excellence Awards.

name: Kopaszi-gát
description: A long Danube embankment in south Buda, created as a regulation dam between 1870 and 1876 to reduce ice floods. After decades of industry and landfill it was redeveloped from 2006 as a landscaped park with cafés, a playground and views across Lágymányos Bay towards the BudaPart quarter.

children.text: Kopaszi-gát takes its name from the Kopaszi sandbank that once lay in this stretch of the Danube; the name can be translated as the bare bank. Ice floes jammed against sandbars here in the 18th and 19th centuries and caused icy floods. After the Pest flood of 1838, a law in 1870 ordered river regulation and a parallel dam, and the long, sandy dam was completed in 1876. Because its southern end did not reach the bank, Lágymányos Bay formed.

The water behind the dam later divided into a bay and Lágymányos Lake. In May 1896 the Orfeum owner Károly Somossy opened Konstantinápoly Budapesten, a Turkish-style entertainment quarter, here; it lost its appeal quickly because of mosquitoes and closed about six months later. In the early 20th century parts of the lake were filled in while the Budapest University of Technology was built, and the rest was used for fish farming, boating and swimming; Alfréd Hajós often trained there. After the Second World War about 1.5 million cubic metres of soil and rubble filled nearly the whole lakebed and factories took over.

After industry closed following the political change, the area deteriorated until around 2000. From 2006 restaurants, bistros and cafés opened, a playground was built and the dam was redeveloped as a green leisure park; one visitor guide says that by 2007 the embankment had become a landscaped public park, with architecture using concrete, metal, wood and glass.

The surroundings keep changing. In 2015 the district sold the bay's embankment and undeveloped land, 57 hectares in all, and the area, now called BudaPart, was planned by the firm ADEPT, which won the 2016 planning competition. The MOL Campus tower, designed by Foster + Partners, is 143 metres tall and employees moved in during December 2022, giving south Buda a new point of orientation.
Good to know
One visitor guide suggests tram 1 to Rákóczi Bridge, then about a 10-minute walk to the entrance; check current routes before you travel.
The Budapest University of Technology and Economics and Rákóczi Bridge are close by, so the park fits a walk along the Danube in south Buda.
Restaurants and cafés have their own times, so check them individually before planning a meal.

historyIntro: Kopaszi-gát began as an engineering response to the ice floods that struck Pest, and over almost 150 years it has been a regulation dam, a lakeshore, an industrial zone and finally a park.

historySections.heading: Ice floods and the regulation dam

children.text: Before the river was regulated, two sandbars, the Nyúlfutási-zátony and the Kopaszi-zátony, narrowed the Danube south of Pest, and ice floes jammed against them in the 18th and 19th centuries. The Kopaszi sandbank was named for its barren appearance. The Pest ice flood of 1838 killed 153 people, destroyed over 10,000 buildings and left at least 50,000 people homeless. The water engineer Pál Vásárhelyi proposed a solution, but Pest's city leaders thought its cost of nearly nine million forints too high and shelved it. In 1870 a law ordered river regulation and a parallel dam, and the long, sandy, treeless dam was completed in 1876.

Because the dam's southern end did not reach the bank, Lágymányos Bay formed. A railway bridge connecting Ferencváros and Kelenföld split the water: the southern half was planned as a winter harbour, and the northern part became Lágymányos Lake. Factories soon followed, making the area one of the capital's industrial centres. In the early 20th century parts of the lake were filled in during the construction of the Budapest University of Technology, and the remaining water was used for fish farming, boating and swimming, with clubs, restaurants, a water polo pitch and an open-air pool. After the Second World War about 1.5 million cubic metres of soil and rubble filled nearly the whole lakebed to support industrialisation, and the recreational area disappeared.

After the regime change local industry closed and the area deteriorated until around 2000. The Aranyhal restaurant, which had operated since the 1970s, closed in 2005. From 2006 restaurants, bistros and cafés opened, a playground was built and the dam was redeveloped as a green leisure park. In 2015 the district sold the bay's embankment and undeveloped land, 57 hectares in all, and the new quarter called BudaPart was planned by ADEPT, which won the planning competition in 2016. The 143-metre MOL Campus, designed by Foster + Partners, received its first employees in December 2022.

stories.title: Konstantinápoly Budapesten, 1896

children.text: In May 1896, the year of the Hungarian millennium celebrations, the Orfeum owner Károly Somossy launched Konstantinápoly Budapesten, a Turkish-style entertainment quarter on the Lágymányos shore. It was designed by Lipót Kellner and Kálmán Gerster.
Its appeal faded quickly because of mosquitoes, and it closed about six months after opening. Somossy went bankrupt.

name: Zugliget Chairlift
description: Hungary's first passenger ropeway, opened on 20 August 1970, carrying double chairs for 1,040 metres from Zugliget up János Hill, a rise of 262 metres. Its nickname Libegő, meaning floater, won a public naming contest, and the top station is a short walk from the Erzsébet lookout.

children.text: The Zugliget Chairlift, known as the Libegő, runs from Zugliget in Budapest's 12th district up János Hill, the highest peak in Budapest. BKK describes it as Hungary's first passenger ropeway and gives its opening as 20 August 1970. The track is 1,040 metres long with a height difference of 262 metres between the stations, and the ride takes 12 to 15 minutes depending on the source. BKK counts 102 double chairs.

The idea is older than the line. In 1933 the engineer István Hantos Jr. proposed a suspension railway from Zugliget to János Hill, but only preparatory work was done, and the plans were revived in the early 1940s before the Second World War halted construction. The 12th District Council decided to build the line in 1967, construction started on 24 March 1969, and it opened in 1970. The official name was Jánoshegyi Légpálya, János Hill Air Lane, but a public naming contest produced the nickname Libegő, which means floater.

At the top, the Erzsébet lookout tower is a few minutes' walk away; Visit Hungary calls it the highest spot in Budapest, and the surrounding hill is covered with forests, gardens and hiking trails. BKK notes that the upper station has a wheelchair-accessible lookout on the terrace of a former restaurant.

The chairlift also links with other Buda hills attractions. BKK says the upper station can be reached on foot from the János-hegy or Virágvölgy stops of the Children's Railway, and by bus 21 or 211 from Széll Kálmán tér to Normafa followed by a walk of 20 to 30 minutes.
Good to know
BKK gives the lower station as Zugligeti út 97, at the terminus of bus 291, which runs from Nyugati pályaudvar.
Passengers with severely limited mobility are not permitted to ride, and children under 10 may ride only with an accompanying adult.
Service can be suspended in severe storms and for maintenance on set dates, so check the BKK page for the current operating service and closure days before you go.
The Erzsébet lookout tower and the Children's Railway stops at János-hegy and Virágvölgy are nearby.

historyIntro: The Zugliget chairlift took almost four decades to move from a proposal to a working line. When it opened in 1970 it was Hungary's first passenger ropeway.

children.text: In 1933 the engineer István Hantos Jr. proposed a suspension railway from Zugliget to János Hill, but only preparatory work was done. In the early 1940s the Metropolitan Tramways Company revived the plans, and the Second World War halted construction. In spring 1945 the idea of a whole rope-railway network resurfaced and an Óbuda to Hármashatárhegy line was planned, but it was not built. In 1967 the 12th District City Council decided to build the János Hill line, with UVATERV providing the professional work.

Construction started on 24 March 1969 under László Pataki, who became the first service manager, with the National Mining Machinery Manufacturer Company as main contractor. The steel pillars were made in Tatabánya, two buildings were demolished to clear the route and the hanging chairs were imported from Austria. BKK gives the opening date as 20 August 1970. The line is 1,040 metres long with a level difference of 262 metres, and BKV reports about 4.5 million passengers in its first ten years.

A new wire rope was installed in 1979. A 1985 action plan proposed an alpine-style catering building at the upper station that was never built, and a reconstruction took place in 1991, with the rope replaced by an Austrian-made one in 1992. A plan in 1997 and 1998 proposed restoring the former János Hill restaurant. BKV's account does not clearly explain how the 1979 rope and the 1991 reconstruction relate, so the sequence of work on the line should be taken from the operator's current information.

stories.title: How the Libegő got its name

children.text: Visit Hungary says the name János Hill Cableway was judged unappealing, so a naming contest followed. Suggestions included Hillicopter, János Hill Hummer, Space Bus and To-and-Fro. The winning name, Libegő, means floater. BKV likewise says the name was chosen in a public naming contest and that the official name is Jánoshegyi Légpálya, János Hill Air Lane.
